title: The ‘dream job’ myth: Why a fulfilling career does not have to define your life
summary: A more sustainable approach sees careers as one part of a meaningful life, not the entire foundation of it.
author: Valerie Onyia Babatope, Assistant Professor of Human Resource Management, MacEwan University
paragraphs: At some point, most of us have heard the same advice about work: find a job you love, and you’ll never work a day in your life.

The idea of a “dream job” sounds inspiring, even noble; it suggests that work can be a source of meaning, identity and personal fulfillment. But this ideal can also create a significant amount of pressure, especially for those just entering the workforce.
If your career does not feel like a calling — or if your interests change over time and your work no longer feels like a perfect fit — it can feel like a personal failure.

But research on careers and motivation suggests the challenge may not be that we’re struggling to find purpose, but that we’ve been taught to expect one job to provide everything: meaning, identity, financial security and personal fulfillment.

Meaningful work can be an important part of a satisfying life. But the relentless pursuit of a single “dream job” can lead to burnout, financial strain and a fragile sense of identity. A more sustainable approach is to view work as one part of a fulfilling life rather than the whole picture.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.

## When loving your job comes at a cost
One challenge with the dream-job ideal is that passion can sometimes create difficult workplace trade-offs.

Research by psychologist Aaron Kay and colleagues suggests that people are more likely to view it as acceptable to place extra demands on passionate workers — including unpaid work, tasks outside their job description and sacrifices of personal time because they assume the work itself provides a form of reward.

This dynamic may be particularly relevant in fields often associated with passion, such as media, fashion, entertainment and the arts, where workers frequently describe their jobs as closely tied to personal identity and creative fulfillment.
Passion can be a source of motivation and satisfaction, but when work is treated as a calling, it can become easier to justify blurred boundaries and unrealistic expectations.
## Tying your identity to work

The second challenge is psychological. The person you are at 22 is unlikely to be the same person you become at 32 or 42. Career development researchers have long argued that occupational identity is not fixed; it develops over time as people’s interests, values and life circumstances change.

But when we build a large part of our identity around a single occupation, career changes can become more difficult. Research on career identity suggests that having a more flexible sense of self can help people navigate transitions, while a narrowly defined professional identity may make change feel more disruptive.

Finally, there is the risk of burnout. When a hobby or personal interest becomes a profession, the activity that once provided relaxation can become tied to deadlines, client and patient feedback, and revenue targets.

When work is also your passion, a difficult day can feel like a personal failure. The pressure to maintain enthusiasm and constantly demonstrate commitment can gradually undermine the motivation that brought someone into the field in the first place.
## A new definition of career success
A growing body of research suggests that many workers are rethinking the traditional idea that career success means finding one perfect occupation.

This shift is particularly visible among Generation Z, the cohort currently entering the workforce. While younger workers are sometimes criticized as being “lazy” or “uncommitted,” they may instead be challenging older assumptions about what a successful career should provide.

A 2025 survey found that financial stability and work-life balance rank among the most important factors for Gen Z and millennials, alongside opportunities for growth and meaningful work. It’s a mindset of “peace over promotion.”

Recruiter and career coach Emily Durham argues we should seek work that meets three core needs: validation (feeling seen and appreciated), purpose (finding meaning) and lifestyle (meeting your financial and personal needs).

Crucially, these needs do not all have to be met by one “dream job.” By looking at the entirety of our lives, we can create more stability and resilience, especially in a world of economic uncertainty and AI-driven change.
## Build a career that can adapt
If the dream-job model is limiting, what should replace it? One alternative is to focus less on finding the perfect job title and more on developing a portfolio of transferable skills.
Instead of anchoring your identity to being a “marketing director,” for example, you could set a goal to master a portfolio of skills like persuasive writing, data analysis and project management.
A skill portfolio is adaptable, allowing you to apply your toolkit to different industries and roles as your passions evolve. It gives you the freedom to pivot without starting over.

Another important part of career development is mentorship. Mentorship is one of the most effective strategies for navigating career decisions and building confidence. My own research shows effective mentoring helps build awareness of career paths and clarify options.

Psychosocial mentoring, meanwhile, provides emotional support and helps individuals decouple their sense of worth from their job titles. This kind of support is invaluable when you are trying to figure out what you want, not just what you can get.
## Work is only one part of a fulfilling life

The relentless pursuit of a “dream job” isn’t the only path to a successful career. In a world where the nature of work is changing faster than ever, the most resilient and fulfilling career path is one that is adaptable.

It starts with building a portfolio of skills, is guided by mentors and is measured not by finding a single perfect job title, but by how well your work fits into a life you are passionate about living.

A fulfilling career does not have to provide every source of purpose and identity. Sometimes, the healthiest relationship with work comes from allowing it to be one meaningful part of a larger, richer life.
